issues.legal_issue: A pleading amendment sought after trial has concluded may be allowed only when the applicant establishes that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised before trial.
material_facts: The claimants brought a suit for specific performance, but their original plaint omitted an averment that they had performed or had always been ready and willing to perform their essential contractual obligations.
The parties completed their evidence and arguments, and the matter was reserved for judgment before the claimants applied to amend the plaint.
The claimants attributed the omission to a typing mistake, although the omitted averment was substantive and could have been noticed and corrected when the plaint was prepared, signed, and verified.

The claimants relied on references to readiness and willingness in a prior legal notice and in their evidence, but the court held that those matters did not satisfy the requirements for allowing the amendment.
issues.conclusion: The amendment should not have been allowed. The explanation of a typing mistake did not establish due diligence, so the High Court’s order allowing the amendment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 CPC permits amendment of pleadings, but its proviso bars an amendment after commencement of trial unless the court is satisfied that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised before trial. Due diligence requires reasonable investigation and cannot be dispensed with. A substantive omission that could have been found by reviewing the pleading is not a typographical error. In a specific-performance suit, Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act requires the claimant to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform; Explanation (ii) requires the relevant averment, and Form 47 in Appendix A to the CPC prescribes it. The amendment rule aims to prevent late amendments, surprise, and delay. The Court referred to Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha, Ajendraprasadji N. Pandey v. Swami Keshavprakeshdasji N., Chander Kanta Bansal v. Rajinder Singh Anand, Rajkumar Guraward v. S.K. Sarwagi and Company Private Limited, Vidyabai v. Padmalatha, and Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and amendment_sought_after_trial and essential_readiness_plea_omitted and omission_preventable_by_ordinary_review and typing_mistake_explanation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.amendment_sought_after_trial: The claimant sought to amend the pleading after the trial and arguments had concluded and the matter had been reserved for decision.
predicates.essential_readiness_plea_omitted: The original pleading did not state that the claimant had performed or had always been ready and willing to perform the claimant’s essential contractual obligations.
predicates.omission_preventable_by_ordinary_review: The omitted substantive averment could have been noticed and included by reviewing the pleading before it was filed.
predicates.typing_mistake_explanation: The claimant attributed the omission to a typing mistake.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a specific-performance suit seeks, after trial, to add an essential averment that could have been included through ordinary review and explains its omission as a typing mistake, the amendment is rejected.
